Strict intake/output supports assessment of kidney function and perfusion and helps evaluate the response to the prescribed diuretic and BP treatment. Output must be interpreted with laboratory trends and the rest of the assessment; increased urination alone does not prove recovery. (Sources: Chapter 31 Brian More case study; teacher outline, Chapter 31. Outline focus: Connect renal findings to strict intake/output monitoring. Slides 118, 119, 123.)

question: One hour after Brian receives his prescribed diuretic and antihypertensives, BP falls from 180/100 to 150/90 mm Hg. Two days later it is 125/80, HR is 72/min, and BUN and creatinine have normalized. Which conclusion is best?
option1: The normal BP establishes that all retinal and ventricular changes have already disappeared
option2: The lower HR alone proves that the renal abnormalities no longer need follow-up
option3: The combined BP, HR, and renal trends support an effective treatment response, with continued long-term management needed
option4: The normal renal tests show that BP medication can now be replaced by the statin alone
rationale: The outline defines improvement through BP and HR normalization together with renal laboratory improvement. These combined trends support treatment effectiveness. They do not establish reversal of structural heart or retinal damage and do not justify stopping prescribed therapy. (Sources: Chapter 31 Brian More case study; teacher outline, Chapter 31. Outline focus: Evaluate response using BP, HR, and renal trends. Slides 119, 131.)

question: Brian's BP and kidney laboratory results improve, but testing shows left ventricular hypertrophy and retinal damage. His daughter asks whether normal BP means follow-up is no longer needed. Which response is best?
option1: Improved BP reduces further injury, but existing heart and eye changes still require ongoing treatment and follow-up
option2: Once kidney laboratory results normalize, the heart and retinal changes are considered resolved as well
option3: Only the eye findings need follow-up because ventricular hypertrophy does not relate to chronic hypertension
option4: Follow-up can wait until he again develops headaches because symptoms reliably indicate uncontrolled BP
rationale: The case identifies ventricular hypertrophy and retinal damage despite improved BP and renal results. The outline emphasizes preventing progression through consistent treatment and follow-up. Hypertension can be asymptomatic, and improvement in one organ system does not prove recovery in every affected organ. (Sources: Chapter 31 Brian More case study; teacher outline, Chapter 31. Outline focus: Interpret organ damage and the need for continued management. Slides 119–120; outline: hypertension complications and adherence.)

question: During discharge teaching, Brian says, "Both my parents died from strokes, so changing my habits probably will not help." Which response best addresses his case-specific risks?
option1: Because both parents had strokes, only his inherited risk matters when planning prevention
option2: His statin removes the vascular effects of smoking, so tobacco cessation is a lower-value goal
option3: Once his BP is controlled, his glucose and lipid levels no longer contribute to vascular risk
option4: Family history cannot be changed, but stopping smoking and managing BP, lipids, glucose, and activity can reduce additional risk
rationale: Brian has a strong family history plus modifiable risks, including smoking, hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes, obesity, and inactivity when present. The outline emphasizes addressing modifiable risks despite age or genetic risk. Medication does not cancel tobacco exposure or make glucose and lipid management unnecessary. (Sources: Chapter 31 Brian More case study; teacher outline, Chapter 31. Outline focus: Teach smoking cessation and distinguish modifiable from nonmodifiable risks. Slides 117–120, 124, 128.)

question: Brian and his daughter are planning meals after discharge. His teaching plan follows the teacher outline's approximately 1,600-mg daily sodium target. Which statement shows the best understanding?
option1: We will avoid the saltshaker, so sodium listed on packaged foods does not need to be counted
option2: We will allow 1,600 mg at each meal because the limit applies separately to breakfast, lunch, and dinner
option3: We will add the sodium in all servings eaten each day and favor fruits, vegetables, and foods low in saturated fat
option4: We will focus only on avoiding sugar because the DASH plan does not address sodium or fat
rationale: The outline specifies an approximately 1,600-mg daily sodium target, not a per-meal allowance. Total sodium includes packaged foods and every serving consumed. DASH teaching also emphasizes fruits, vegetables, and lower saturated fat. Diabetes management and BP-focused nutrition both remain relevant for Brian. (Sources: Chapter 31 Brian More case study; teacher outline, Chapter 31. Outline focus: Apply DASH and daily sodium teaching. Slides 28–29, 120, 124.)

question: At discharge, Brian explains how he will manage his medications and activity. Which statement requires the nurse to reteach the plan before he leaves?
option1: I will sit up first and stand slowly, and I will ask for help if I become dizzy
option2: If I feel well and my home BP is normal, I will skip the BP drugs and restart them when I have a headache
option3: I will record my home BP and bring the readings to the planned follow-up visits
option4: I will take the medications on the prescribed schedule and follow any specific hold instructions
rationale: Symptom-based or occasional dosing conflicts with the teacher outline. Normal readings may reflect effective medication, and hypertension can cause damage without symptoms. Slow position changes, home monitoring, planned follow-up, and adherence within prescribed parameters fit Brian's discharge plan. (Sources: Chapter 31 Brian More case study; teacher outline, Chapter 31. Outline focus: Assess adherence and orthostatic safety through teach-back. Slides 120, 124–125.)

question: A client with unstable BP requires frequent titration of a vasoactive infusion and repeated ABG sampling. Which monitoring device most directly meets these needs?
option1: A routine intermittent temperature probe
option2: An arterial catheter
option3: A central venous catheter used only for CVP
option4: A peripheral pulse oximeter alone
rationale: An arterial catheter provides continuous BP measurement and access for arterial blood sampling. CVP assesses right-sided filling pressure, while pulse oximetry estimates saturation rather than directly measuring BP or arterial gases. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Hemodynamic monitoring: arterial line; slides 5–10.)

question: After repositioning a client, the arterial pressure abruptly changes even though the cuff pressure and clinical assessment are unchanged. The transducer was not moved. What should the nurse check first?
option1: Whether the transducer remains level with the phlebostatic axis
option2: Whether the client needs a routine fluid bolus based only on the displayed number
option3: Whether the next vasopressor dose can be doubled immediately
option4: Whether the arterial catheter should be removed without inspecting the setup
rationale: A change in the transducer's height relative to the client can distort pressure readings. Re-level and validate the system before making treatment changes based on an unexplained discrepancy. Always correlate the monitor with the client. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Hemodynamic monitoring: leveling after repositioning; slide 7 and outline.)

question: The nurse prepares to zero an invasive pressure transducer. Which sequence is correct?
option1: Administer a fluid bolus, record the highest reading, and label that value as zero
option2: Open the patient catheter directly to air, flush blood out, and then zero the monitor
option3: Isolate the patient from the open port, open the transducer to air, zero, then restore measurement to the patient
option4: Zero while the transducer is closed to atmospheric pressure and leave the patient connection off
rationale: Zeroing establishes atmospheric pressure as the reference while the patient is isolated from the open port. The system is then returned to patient measurement. The client's catheter must not be opened directly to air. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Hemodynamic monitoring: zeroing; condensed deck page 3 and outline.)

question: An arterial waveform is blunted, the dicrotic notch is difficult to see, and systolic pressure reads lower than the cuff value. Which interpretation is most likely?
option1: An underdamped monitoring system
option2: A normal waveform that proves the cuff is inaccurate
option3: A waveform that independently confirms cardiogenic shock
option4: An overdamped monitoring system
rationale: A blunted waveform and reduced systolic amplitude suggest overdamping. Assess the client and inspect the system for causes such as air, obstruction, or inappropriate tubing. A distorted signal cannot independently establish the shock diagnosis. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Hemodynamic monitoring: waveform troubleshooting; slide 10 and outline.)

question: An arterial tracing has unusually tall peaks with repeated ringing. The arterial systolic reading is much higher than the cuff reading, while the client appears unchanged. What should the nurse do?
option1: Immediately increase antihypertensive treatment without validating the waveform
option2: Document the arterial systolic number as unquestionably accurate because the line is invasive
option3: Assume the ringing indicates a new atrial dysrhythmia and ignore the pressure setup
option4: Evaluate an underdamped system before titrating treatment solely to the exaggerated systolic value
rationale: Underdamping can exaggerate systolic pressure and cause ringing. Validate the setup and dynamic response and correlate with clinical and cuff findings. An invasive measurement is not automatically reliable when its waveform is distorted. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Hemodynamic monitoring: underdamping; slide 10 and outline.)

question: A client has a central venous catheter used to measure CVP. Which interpretation of that measurement is appropriate?
option1: It directly measures left ventricular ejection fraction
option2: It reflects right atrial pressure and contributes to assessment of right-sided filling
option3: It identifies the exact coronary artery causing an MI
option4: It independently measures the amount of oxygen remaining in pulmonary venous blood
rationale: CVP reflects right atrial pressure and provides information about right-sided filling. Interpret it with the broader clinical picture; it is not a direct measure of EF, coronary anatomy, or pulmonary venous oxygenation. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Hemodynamic monitoring: central venous pressure; slides 11–12.)

question: During pulmonary artery catheter insertion, the team observes changing pressure waveforms as the catheter advances. Which sequence is anatomically correct?
option1: Pulmonary artery, aorta, right atrium, then left ventricle
option2: Left ventricle, right ventricle, pulmonary artery, then vena cava
option3: Right atrium, left atrium, left ventricle, then the aorta
option4: Right atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary artery, then an occlusion waveform when appropriately wedged
rationale: The catheter travels through the right side of the heart into the pulmonary artery. Appropriate temporary balloon occlusion produces the wedge/PAOP tracing. The catheter does not pass through the left heart during this route. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Hemodynamic monitoring: PA catheter path; slides 13–15.)

question: A client after a large LV infarction has CO 2.1 L/min, high PAOP, high SVR, and low SvO2. Which interpretation best integrates these findings?
option1: A high-output state with excessive systemic vasodilation
option2: Normal systemic perfusion because elevated filling pressure guarantees adequate output
option3: Primary hypovolemia with low cardiac filling pressures
option4: Low-output LV pump failure with congestion and compensatory vasoconstriction
rationale: Low CO with high left-sided filling pressure and high SVR fits cardiogenic shock from LV failure. Low SvO2 supports inadequate delivery relative to tissue demand. High filling pressure does not mean the heart is ejecting effectively. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Hemodynamic profiles: cardiogenic shock; slides 55, 64, 72.)

question: Two clients are hypotensive. Client A has low CO, high PAOP, and crackles after MI. Client B has low CO and low filling pressures after major blood loss. Which distinction is most useful?
option1: Both have identical volume deficits because every low BP requires the same fluid treatment
option2: Client A has a congested failing pump; Client B has inadequate circulating volume
option3: Client A has distributive shock because crackles prove low SVR
option4: Client B has cardiogenic shock because any reduction in CO indicates myocardial failure
rationale: Low BP and low CO occur through different mechanisms. Elevated filling pressure with pulmonary congestion after MI favors pump failure; blood loss with low filling pressure favors hypovolemia. Treatment must reflect the cause and congestion status. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Hemodynamic monitoring: compare shock states; teacher outline.)

question: In a low-output client after MI, SvO2 falls from 65% to 48% while oxygen delivery remains inadequate. What does this trend suggest?
option1: The sample proves that all tissues are receiving sufficient oxygen
option2: Cardiac output has necessarily doubled because venous saturation fell
option3: Tissues are extracting a larger fraction of delivered oxygen in a low-flow state
option4: The lungs are transferring too much oxygen and should receive less inspired oxygen immediately
rationale: Low SvO2 can reflect increased extraction when oxygen delivery is inadequate relative to demand. Interpret the trend with CO, hemoglobin, arterial oxygenation, and clinical perfusion rather than assuming a single cause or changing oxygen blindly. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Hemodynamic monitoring: SvO2 in cardiogenic shock; slide 64.)

question: A client with diabetes reports new jaw pressure, nausea, diaphoresis, and shortness of breath but denies severe central chest pain. Which action is most appropriate?
option1: Reassure the client that MI requires severe central chest pain
option2: Arrange routine outpatient testing because the symptoms are atypical
option3: Assess for acute coronary syndrome and obtain the ordered urgent ECG
option4: Delay cardiac assessment until gastrointestinal medication fails
rationale: MI can present with jaw discomfort, nausea, sweating, dyspnea, or fatigue. Absence of severe central chest pain does not exclude ACS, especially in a high-risk client. Prompt assessment and ECG help prevent delay. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Myocardial infarction: presentation and diagnosis; slides 17, 20–21.)

question: A client has ischemic chest discomfort, ST depression, and a rising troponin above the laboratory reference range. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
option1: NSTEMI is a concern because ischemic symptoms accompany evidence of myocardial injury without ST elevation
option2: Stable angina is confirmed because ST depression always occurs without tissue injury
option3: Unstable angina is established because any absence of ST elevation excludes necrosis
option4: The troponin result is irrelevant because only ST elevation can identify an infarction
rationale: In the stated ischemic setting, a troponin rise indicates myocardial injury consistent with NSTEMI. Unstable angina does not have biomarker evidence of necrosis. Troponin must be interpreted in clinical context rather than as a stand-alone diagnosis. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Myocardial infarction: ACS spectrum; slides 18–22.)

question: A client has new ischemic chest pain at rest. Serial troponins remain below the injury threshold and the team diagnoses unstable angina. Which explanation best distinguishes this from MI?
option1: There is no coronary risk because the troponin remains below the threshold
option2: There is myocardial necrosis that is excluded only when ST elevation appears
option3: There is myocardial ischemia without demonstrated myocardial necrosis
option4: There is complete recovery, so recurrence of symptoms does not need urgent reporting
rationale: Unstable angina involves ischemic symptoms without biomarker evidence of infarction. It remains an acute coronary syndrome requiring evaluation and treatment. Negative troponins do not make new rest symptoms harmless. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Myocardial infarction: unstable angina versus infarction; slide 19.)

question: A client with ongoing ischemic chest pain has a diagnostic STEMI ECG. The catheterization team is available. Which action best addresses the cause of threatened muscle loss?
option1: Focus only on pain relief once the client reports less discomfort
option2: Prepare promptly for prescribed PCI while continuing stabilization and monitoring
option3: Wait for serial troponin results to peak before preparing for reperfusion
option4: Delay intervention until a routine outpatient stress test identifies exercise tolerance
rationale: STEMI requires rapid reperfusion to restore flow and limit myocardial death. Stabilization and symptom control support care but do not replace opening the obstructed artery. Troponin peak should not be awaited when the diagnosis and treatment pathway are established. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Myocardial infarction: reperfusion and PCI; slides 23–26.)

question: A client with acute MI has SpO2 84% and respiratory distress. Prescribed oxygen, aspirin, and anti-ischemic medications are available. Which action is the immediate priority?
option1: Delay oxygen until the complete cardiac enzyme panel returns
option2: Treat pain alone and assume oxygenation will normalize when pain decreases
option3: Apply oxygen and support breathing while proceeding with the other urgent ACS care
option4: Give the oral statin before addressing the low oxygen saturation
rationale: The outline prioritizes correction of hypoxemia in MI. Clear hypoxemia with distress requires immediate support while other time-sensitive ACS interventions proceed. This does not mean that oxygen is automatically indicated for every normoxemic chest-pain client. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Myocardial infarction: hypoxemia and order priorities; outline.)

question: A client with ACS asks why aspirin was prescribed along with nitroglycerin. Which explanation is best?
option1: Aspirin directly dissolves the existing clot, while nitroglycerin replaces reperfusion
option2: Aspirin reduces platelet aggregation, while nitroglycerin helps reduce ischemic symptoms and cardiac workload
option3: Both medications reverse myocardial necrosis within minutes of administration
option4: Aspirin raises the heart rate, while nitroglycerin permanently repairs damaged muscle
rationale: The drugs have different roles. Aspirin limits platelet aggregation; nitroglycerin can improve ischemic symptoms through vascular effects and reduced workload. Neither reverses established necrosis or replaces indicated reperfusion. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Myocardial infarction: medication purposes; slides 23–24, 35.)

question: Before a scheduled IV beta-blocker dose after MI, a client's BP is 78/46 mm Hg, with cool skin and new confusion. What is the best action?
option1: Withhold the dose pending urgent evaluation and notify the provider of possible shock
option2: Administer an extra dose because the sympathetic response must be eliminated immediately
option3: Give the dose and postpone the next assessment until its peak effect
option4: Give the dose because reducing HR is always the first priority after MI
rationale: Beta blockers can reduce myocardial workload in suitable patients, but new shock and hypotension require reassessment. Additional suppression of rate or contractility could worsen perfusion. Medication purpose does not override current hemodynamic contraindications. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Myocardial infarction: beta blockers; cardiogenic shock assessment.)

question: A client with STEMI cannot receive timely PCI, and the team considers fibrinolysis. Which finding requires immediate clarification before treatment?
option1: Current significant gastrointestinal bleeding
option2: An elevated troponin with ischemic ECG changes
option3: A history of treated hypertension with a currently stable BP
option4: Chest discomfort beginning shortly before arrival
rationale: Fibrinolysis can cause major bleeding and requires eligibility and contraindication screening. Active significant bleeding is a major concern. The other findings do not by themselves establish this bleeding contraindication. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Myocardial infarction: fibrinolysis and reperfusion selection.)

question: After CABG, a client's chest tube output abruptly increases to 260 mL of bright-red blood in one hour, and BP begins falling. Which action is most appropriate?
option1: Begin ambulation to stimulate drainage before notifying the surgeon
option2: Notify the surgical team immediately and assess for hemorrhage and impaired perfusion
option3: Clamp the chest tubes to keep circulating blood inside the chest
option4: Document the drainage as expected and wait for the next routine blood count
rationale: A sudden bright-red increase with falling BP raises concern for postoperative hemorrhage. Prompt surgical evaluation and hemodynamic assessment are required. Clamping does not correct blood loss and may cause dangerous accumulation. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Post-CABG: chest drainage and hemodynamics; slide 34.)

question: A post-CABG client produces 18 mL of urine in one hour and 20 mL in the next. The urinary catheter is patent. Which response best follows the course guidance?
option1: Wait until complete anuria occurs before reporting a possible renal problem
option2: Remove fluid limits and encourage a large oral intake without assessing congestion
option3: Continue routine monitoring because any urine output rules out a perfusion problem
option4: Notify the provider and assess cardiac output, BP, and renal status
rationale: The slides call for reporting urine output below 30 mL/hour for two hours. With obstruction excluded, low output may reflect impaired renal perfusion or injury. Evaluate the hemodynamic context rather than assuming a fluid deficit. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Post-CABG: renal surveillance; slide 34.)

question: A client returning from CABG is hypothermic and shivering. Why should rewarming be controlled and shivering addressed?
option1: Rapid warming prevents every dysrhythmia and is preferred regardless of BP
option2: Shivering is needed to protect the grafts, so analgesia and warming should be withheld
option3: Shivering increases oxygen demand, while overly rapid warming can cause vasodilation and hypotension
option4: Temperature has no meaningful effect on myocardial workload after surgery
rationale: The chapter recommends gradual rewarming and prevention of shivering. Shivering raises metabolic demand, and rapid warming can contribute to hypotension or dysrhythmia. Monitor temperature and hemodynamic response together. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Post-CABG: rewarming; slides 33, 36.)

question: An extubated, stable post-CABG client avoids coughing because of incisional pain. Which plan best supports pulmonary recovery?
option1: Provide prescribed analgesia, teach incision splinting, and assist coughing, deep breathing, and early mobility
option2: Suppress all coughing until the incision has completely healed
option3: Maintain strict bed rest and delay pulmonary hygiene until discharge
option4: Encourage only shallow breathing to avoid increasing chest discomfort
rationale: Pain control and splinting make effective coughing and deep breathing more tolerable. Pulmonary hygiene and appropriate early mobility reduce respiratory and immobility complications. Avoidance of these activities can worsen secretion retention and atelectasis. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Post-CABG: pulmonary hygiene and mobility; slide 36.)

question: A client with dilated cardiomyopathy asks why a low ejection fraction causes fatigue and dyspnea. Which explanation is most accurate?
option1: Low ejection fraction indicates only a slow heart rate with normal contraction
option2: An enlarged ventricle necessarily pumps more blood with every beat
option3: Weakened ventricular contraction reduces forward flow and can cause congestion
option4: Cardiomyopathy affects the vessels but cannot alter heart-muscle function
rationale: Dilated cardiomyopathy can weaken systolic contraction, reducing effective output and promoting congestion. Chamber enlargement does not guarantee a larger effective stroke volume. EF reflects the fraction ejected, not heart rate alone. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Cardiomyopathy: structural and functional changes; slides 40–43.)

question: A client with cardiomyopathy asks why an ACE inhibitor, a beta blocker, and a diuretic are prescribed together. Which response best matches the outline?
option1: They cure the structural disease once the first normal BP reading is obtained
option2: They all act only as anticoagulants to prevent ventricular clots
option3: They address workload and remodeling through different mechanisms, while the diuretic reduces excess volume
option4: They serve identical purposes, so taking any one replaces the other two
rationale: The prescribed regimen addresses different contributors to symptoms and progression. ACE inhibition and beta blockade affect workload and neurohormonal mechanisms; diuretics manage congestion. They are not interchangeable and do not cure the underlying structural disease. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Cardiomyopathy: combined medication rationale; teacher outline.)

question: A client with cardiomyopathy and ventricular dyssynchrony is scheduled for a resynchronization pacemaker. What benefit is the team primarily seeking?
option1: More coordinated ventricular contraction to improve pumping efficiency
option2: Permanent elimination of the need for heart-failure medications
option3: Removal of an obstructing coronary plaque through the pacing leads
option4: Treatment of venous valve incompetence by increasing the heart rate
rationale: Resynchronization pacing aims to coordinate ventricular contraction in selected patients with dyssynchrony. This may improve function but does not remove coronary plaque, repair peripheral veins, or automatically replace medical therapy. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Cardiomyopathy: device therapy for dyssynchrony; outline.)

question: A client with cardiomyopathy says, "Now that I have an ICD, the weak heart muscle is fixed and I can stop my medicines." Which response is best?
option1: Medicines are needed only if the ICD delivers a shock that day
option2: The ICD replaces all medication because it continuously strengthens the ventricle
option3: The device prevents every episode of fluid overload regardless of diet or medication
option4: The ICD treats dangerous rhythms; your structural heart disease still needs the prescribed treatment
rationale: An ICD detects and treats potentially lethal ventricular rhythms. It does not cure cardiomyopathy or prevent every consequence of pump dysfunction. Continuing the individualized medication and self-care plan remains essential. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Cardiomyopathy: ICD purpose and limitations; outline.)

question: A client with cardiomyopathy and an implanted device reports new palpitations and near-syncope. Which response is most appropriate?
option1: Reassure the client that an implanted device makes serious dysrhythmia impossible
option2: Promptly assess rhythm and perfusion and notify the treating team
option3: Arrange routine follow-up only if the symptoms continue for several weeks
option4: Treat the symptoms as proof of successful device function without assessment
rationale: New palpitations with near-syncope may indicate electrical instability or inadequate perfusion and need prompt evaluation. A pacemaker or ICD does not make symptoms benign or establish that the device has corrected the problem. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Cardiomyopathy: complication cues; teacher outline.)

question: A client with cardiomyopathy has worsening orthopnea, increasing edema, and declining activity tolerance. Which interpretation should guide the nurse's response?
option1: The pattern suggests worsening congestion and requires reassessment of the care plan
option2: The edema makes respiratory assessment unnecessary because the problem is peripheral
option3: The client should independently double every cardiac medication
option4: The findings show that ventricular remodeling has fully resolved
rationale: Worsening breathlessness when lying down, edema, and reduced tolerance suggest deterioration in cardiac function or fluid balance. The nurse should evaluate and communicate changes, not assume recovery or recommend unsupervised dose changes. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Cardiomyopathy: assessment, teaching, and outcomes; slides 51–54.)

question: A client after MI has BP 80/48 mm Hg, tachycardia, cool clammy skin, crackles, oliguria, and confusion. Which mechanism best explains the suspected shock?
option1: Impaired myocardial contractility produces inadequate cardiac output and tissue perfusion
option2: Loss of circulating blood volume is necessarily the primary cause of every post-MI low BP
option3: Peripheral vasodilation has eliminated ventricular filling pressure
option4: A high cardiac output is shunting too much oxygen toward peripheral tissues
rationale: The post-MI picture with congestion and systemic hypoperfusion supports cardiogenic shock from pump failure. Hypovolemia and distributive mechanisms differ and require their own supporting evidence. Shock cannot be classified from BP alone. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Cardiogenic shock: mechanism and recognition; slides 55, 64.)

question: A client with cardiogenic shock has pH 7.25, HCO3 17 mEq/L, and elevated lactate. What is the best interpretation?
option1: The low bicarbonate proves isolated respiratory acidosis from CO2 retention
option2: Inadequate tissue perfusion is contributing to anaerobic metabolism and metabolic acidosis
option3: The laboratory pattern establishes normal tissue oxygen delivery
option4: The lactate rise is a desired effect showing restored cardiac output
rationale: Low pH with reduced bicarbonate and elevated lactate supports metabolic acidosis associated with inadequate perfusion. It is a warning of tissue oxygen-delivery failure, not an indicator of successful compensation. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Cardiogenic shock: metabolic and lactic acidosis; slides 55, 57, 64.)

question: A client with cardiogenic shock has low CO and high SVR. A student asks why vasoconstriction occurs when the ventricle is already struggling. Which explanation is best?
option1: High SVR proves that the original shock mechanism was fluid loss
option2: High SVR means the body has stopped all compensatory activity
option3: Vasoconstriction permanently repairs injured myocardial cells
option4: Sympathetic compensation supports pressure but can increase afterload and myocardial workload
rationale: Reduced output triggers sympathetic vasoconstriction and tachycardia. These may support pressure but increase workload and can reinforce ischemia. The compensatory pattern does not by itself establish hypovolemia. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Cardiogenic shock: compensatory cycle; slides 55, 64.)

question: A client with cardiogenic shock is prescribed norepinephrine and dobutamine. Which comparison is most accurate?
option1: Both drugs lower BP solely by causing profound venous pooling
option2: Norepinephrine dissolves the coronary clot; dobutamine prevents platelet aggregation
option3: Dobutamine replaces oxygen therapy, while norepinephrine repairs ventricular scar tissue
option4: Norepinephrine supports vascular tone and BP; dobutamine primarily improves contractility and output
rationale: The case and outline distinguish vasopressor support from inotropic support. Norepinephrine supports BP through vascular effects; dobutamine is used to improve contractility. Both require close monitoring and neither reperfuses an occluded coronary artery by dissolving clot. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Cardiogenic shock: vasoactive and inotropic roles; slides 58, 65, 71.)

question: A client with LV cardiogenic shock has high PAOP, diffuse crackles, and worsening hypoxemia. An additional large fluid bolus is proposed. What is the best nursing response?
option1: Clarify the bolus in light of high filling pressure and pulmonary congestion
option2: Use normal body temperature as proof that excess fluid cannot cause harm
option3: Ignore the PAOP because it never contributes to fluid decisions
option4: Give it rapidly because every shock state requires identical volume loading
rationale: The chapter limits fluid replacement to appropriate circumstances such as low filling pressures. With high filling pressure and congestion, indiscriminate volume can worsen pulmonary edema. The plan should be clarified using the complete clinical and hemodynamic picture. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Cardiogenic shock: fluid decisions; slide 65.)

question: An IABP is being used for a client with cardiogenic shock. Which timing best describes its intended assistance?
option1: Inflate during systolic ejection and remain inflated throughout diastole
option2: Remain continuously inflated to block aortic flow
option3: Deflate only when the client develops a ventricular dysrhythmia
option4: Inflate during diastole and deflate just before systolic ejection
rationale: Diastolic inflation augments coronary perfusion; deflation before systolic ejection reduces resistance to LV ejection. The timing distinguishes counterpulsation from continuous balloon inflation, which would obstruct rather than assist flow. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Mechanical support: IABP; slides 59–60, 65.)

question: A client with a femoral IABP bends the affected knee and raises the head of the bed to 60 degrees. What should the nurse do?
option1: Encourage the position because hip flexion improves balloon timing
option2: Remove the monitoring leads so movement does not trigger alarms
option3: Leave the position unchanged as long as the client reports no pain
option4: Restore the prescribed position with the affected leg straight and head elevation within the device protocol
rationale: The course specifies a straight affected leg and head elevation no more than 30 degrees for the described femoral IABP setup. Positioning protects catheter placement and function. Follow the device and institutional protocol rather than comfort alone. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Mechanical support: IABP nursing safeguards; slide 65.)

question: During IABP care, the cannulated-side foot becomes cool and pale with a diminished pedal pulse compared with the previous assessment. Which action is appropriate?
option1: Promptly assess limb perfusion and notify the team of possible catheter-related ischemia
option2: Document the change as expected because all IABPs eliminate pedal pulses
option3: Massage the calf vigorously and defer vascular reassessment
option4: Wait until the client develops paralysis before reporting the change
rationale: A femoral arterial device can compromise distal circulation. New color, temperature, and pulse changes require prompt assessment and escalation to protect the limb. Pain or paralysis need not be present before reporting ischemic cues. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Mechanical support: distal perfusion assessment; slide 65.)

question: An Impella is placed for severe LV pump failure. Which explanation best describes the support it provides?
option1: It moves blood from the LV into the aorta, unloading the ventricle and supporting forward flow
option2: It drains the right ventricle into the left atrium to bypass the lungs
option3: It provides only an electrical stimulus and cannot support blood flow directly
option4: It permanently replaces the heart muscle with functioning tissue
rationale: Impella is a mechanical pump that draws blood from the LV and delivers it into the aorta, reducing LV work and supporting systemic flow. It does not heal the myocardium directly or function solely as an electrical pacing device. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Mechanical support: Impella; slides 72, 78 and outline.)

question: Despite reperfusion and medication support, a client remains in severe cardiogenic shock. The team discusses temporary mechanical support. Which explanation is most appropriate?
option1: It is used only when the heart is structurally normal and CO is high
option2: It guarantees full myocardial recovery and removes the need for further assessment
option3: It replaces every need to monitor oxygenation, renal function, and neurologic status
option4: It can support circulation as a bridge to recovery or a further definitive treatment decision
rationale: Mechanical circulatory support may stabilize perfusion while recovery or advanced therapy is assessed. It does not guarantee recovery or eliminate monitoring. The outline includes IABP, VAD, ECMO, and transplant consideration for selected refractory cases. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Cardiogenic shock: advanced support; slide 59 and outline.)

question: During shock treatment, BP rises only after a large increase in vasopressor dose, while CO remains low, lactate rises, and urine output falls. Which conclusion is best?
option1: The rising lactate confirms that vasopressor therapy has normalized oxygen delivery
option2: The BP increase proves that shock has resolved even though organ indicators deteriorate
option3: A higher BP alone does not establish recovery; tissue-perfusion findings are worsening
option4: The falling urine output is reassuring because the kidneys need less blood during recovery
rationale: Evaluate the support required to achieve BP together with output and organ-perfusion trends. Rising lactate and falling urine suggest ongoing hypoperfusion despite a higher displayed pressure. This needs prompt reassessment. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Cardiogenic shock: integrated evaluation; slides 64–65, 73.)

question: A client recovering from cardiogenic shock begins basic ADLs, sleeps comfortably, and expresses more control over recovery. Hemodynamics remain stable on reduced support. What do these findings indicate?
option1: Evidence that additional symptom reporting is unnecessary
option2: Functional and physiologic improvement consistent with the care goals
option3: A reason to stop every medication immediately
option4: Complete reversal of all coronary disease with no need for follow-up
rationale: The outline includes return to ADLs, comfortable sleep, and a sense of control as recovery indicators. Stable physiology on less support strengthens that assessment, while long-term treatment and follow-up remain important. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Cardiogenic shock: evaluating recovery; slide 67.)

question: Martin King arrives with crushing chest pain radiating to the left shoulder, diaphoresis, nausea, BP 105/60 mm Hg, HR 110/min, and SpO2 90%. In the supplied case, which prescribed order has first priority?
option1: Begin long-term dietary counseling before administering acute treatment
option2: Delay all treatment until the troponin result returns
option3: Apply the prescribed oxygen while continuing urgent ACS assessment
option4: Give morphine before assessing oxygenation or response to ordered nitroglycerin
rationale: The supplied case and teacher outline prioritize oxygenation in this presentation. The case explicitly orders oxygen and identifies it as the first action among its options. Other acute ACS measures remain time-sensitive; this case-specific ordering is not a rule to give oxygen to every normoxemic MI client. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Martin King case: slides 68, 75; outline: initial order priority.)

question: Martin's ECG shows ST elevation in V1 and V2, and the case reports troponin 12. Which interpretation best matches the supplied case?
option1: An isolated inferior-wall pattern without evidence of myocardial injury
option2: Unstable angina because ST elevation excludes myocardial necrosis
option3: An anteroseptal/septal injury pattern with biomarker evidence supporting acute MI
option4: A normal ECG because only limb leads can show infarction
rationale: The case identifies the V1–V2 pattern as anteroseptal MI; these leads reflect the septal region. In the case context, the elevated troponin supports injury. The ECG and biomarker findings are interpreted together with his ischemic symptoms. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Martin King case: slide 70; outline: ECG/troponin interpretation.)

question: Before Martin deteriorates, metoprolol is given cautiously. Which intended effect best explains this early order?
option1: Increase systemic vascular resistance as the main treatment for shock
option2: Reduce heart rate and myocardial oxygen demand when hemodynamically appropriate
option3: Dissolve the coronary thrombus before angiography
option4: Increase contractility in the same way as dobutamine
rationale: The case uses beta blockade to reduce sympathetic effects and cardiac workload. This role differs from a vasopressor, fibrinolytic, or inotrope. Caution is essential because developing hypotension or shock changes the medication assessment. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Martin King case: slides 69, 76; outline: medication purpose.)

question: Martin's BP falls to 75/50 mm Hg, HR increases to 115/min, and he becomes agitated with cool, pale extremities. Which interpretation should guide immediate care?
option1: The lower BP indicates reduced cardiac workload and successful recovery
option2: He is showing systemic hypoperfusion consistent with cardiogenic shock after MI
option3: The agitation alone establishes an anxiety attack without circulatory compromise
option4: The findings prove hemorrhagic shock even though no blood loss is described
rationale: After MI, hypotension with cool skin and altered mentation strongly suggests inadequate cardiac output and tissue perfusion. The case identifies this deterioration as cardiogenic shock. Anxiety alone or an assumed blood loss does not explain the full picture. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Martin King case: slide 70; outline: recognize shock transition.)

question: During Martin's deterioration, ABGs are pH 7.23, PaCO2 34 mm Hg, PaO2 48 mm Hg, and HCO3 18 mEq/L. Which interpretation matches the case and outline?
option1: Primary hypercapnic failure because PaCO2 is markedly elevated
option2: Hypoxemia with a metabolic acidosis component consistent with impaired tissue perfusion
option3: Adequate oxygenation with isolated respiratory alkalosis
option4: Normal acid-base status because both PaCO2 and bicarbonate are below normal
rationale: The low PaO2 demonstrates hypoxemia; low pH with reduced bicarbonate supports a metabolic acidosis component. In this shock context, anaerobic metabolism from poor perfusion is the key concern. The provided values do not support calling this isolated CO2 retention or a normal ABG. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Martin King case: slide 70; outline: hypoxemia and metabolic acidosis.)

question: Martin is started on norepinephrine and dobutamine, intubated, and transported for PCI. Which explanation best connects these interventions?
option1: Support oxygenation and perfusion while restoring coronary flow to address the precipitating ischemia
option2: Use medications to permanently replace reperfusion because the heart is too weak to benefit
option3: Normalize laboratory values before considering any attempt to open the coronary artery
option4: Treat presumed volume loss without addressing the infarction
rationale: The case combines stabilization with rapid reperfusion: ventilation supports gas exchange, norepinephrine supports BP, dobutamine supports contraction, and PCI restores coronary flow. These complementary actions address both immediate failure and its ischemic cause. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Martin King case: slide 71; outline: actions during deterioration.)

question: After PCI and Impella placement, Martin has CO 2 L/min, PAOP 20 mm Hg, SVR 1,800, and SvO2 50%. Which assessment is most accurate?
option1: He has a high-output distributive pattern because the SVR is reduced
option2: He has isolated volume depletion because the PAOP is low
option3: He still has low output, elevated filling pressure, and inadequate oxygen delivery relative to demand
option4: Normal perfusion is established because coronary intervention has already been completed
rationale: The post-PCI numbers continue to fit cardiogenic shock: low CO, high PAOP and SVR, and low SvO2. Completing PCI does not immediately guarantee recovery of myocardial function or tissue perfusion. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Martin King case: slide 72; outline: hemodynamic profile.)

question: Martin remains on an Impella CP after PCI. Which family explanation best follows the case and teacher outline?
option1: The device pumps blood from the LV to the aorta to unload the weak ventricle while recovery is assessed
option2: The device only monitors pressure and does not provide circulatory assistance
option3: The device repairs all damaged muscle immediately and makes coronary follow-up unnecessary
option4: The device moves blood from the aorta backward into the right ventricle
rationale: The case identifies Impella as support for forward flow and reduced LV workload. The outline describes LV unloading. It is a temporary support strategy in this scenario, not proof of complete myocardial repair. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Martin King case: slides 72, 78; outline: mechanical support.)

question: Martin's BP improves to 105/65 mm Hg as norepinephrine is reduced. CO rises from 2 to 4 L/min, and PAOP falls from 20 to 16 after prescribed Lasix. Which conclusion is best?
option1: Lower PAOP proves that all further diuretic and hemodynamic assessment can stop
option2: The original shock diagnosis was incorrect because the client responded to treatment
option3: Reduced norepinephrine means CO must also be falling regardless of the measured value
option4: Perfusion and congestion trends support improvement while ongoing monitoring remains necessary
rationale: Higher CO and adequate BP on less vasopressor support favor recovery. The PAOP decrease after diuresis supports reduced filling pressure. The combination is more informative than any isolated number and does not remove the need for reassessment. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Martin King case: slide 73; outline: evaluate recovery.)

question: Two days later, Martin's ABGs improve to pH 7.37, PaCO2 38 mm Hg, PaO2 85 mm Hg, and HCO3 24 mEq/L. CO is now 4 L/min with less vasopressor support. Which interpretation is best?
option1: The normal pH alone proves that all cardiac and pulmonary support can be stopped immediately
option2: The combined acid-base, oxygenation, and output trends support improving systemic perfusion
option3: The PaO2 increase is evidence of deterioration because tissue oxygen extraction must have stopped
option4: The bicarbonate change establishes recurrent infarction without needing ECG or clinical data
rationale: The case describes resolution of the metabolic acidosis pattern and improved oxygenation alongside better flow and reduced support. These integrated findings support recovery. They do not independently determine extubation, device removal, or medication discontinuation. (Sources: Chapter 32 slides and teacher outline: Martin King case: slide 73; outline: recovery and ABG trends.)

question: A client with untreated hypertension has BP 214/126 mm Hg, new confusion, blurred vision, and creatinine that increased from 0.9 to 2.3 mg/dL. Which interpretation should guide the nurse's immediate plan?
option1: Severe asymptomatic hypertension requiring routine follow-up
option2: Chronic hypertension with expected age-related renal changes
option3: Hypertensive emergency with acute target-organ injury
option4: Anxiety-related hypertension requiring observation only
rationale: The new neurologic changes and acute creatinine increase indicate target-organ injury accompanying severe hypertension. This requires emergency treatment and monitoring. The BP number alone does not distinguish emergency from severe hypertension without acute injury. (Source: Ch31 slides 27, 118, 121; teacher outline: hypertensive crisis.)

question: The nurse receives reports on four clients. Which client should be assessed first?
option1: A client with BP 198/120 mm Hg and new right-arm weakness and slurred speech
option2: A client with BP 206/116 mm Hg, no symptoms, and an unchanged neurologic examination
option3: A client with BP 168/96 mm Hg and a history of stable chronic kidney disease
option4: A client with BP 156/90 mm Hg who requests teaching about a low-sodium diet
rationale: New focal neurologic deficits suggest acute cerebral injury and require immediate stroke evaluation. They take priority over a higher BP reading without evidence of acute injury. Chronic disease and teaching needs do not have the same immediate urgency. (Source: Ch31 slides 27, 59, 61; teacher outline: priority assessments.)

question: A client with a confirmed hypertensive emergency is on continuous monitoring, has patent IV access, and has SpO2 97% on room air. Which prescribed intervention should the nurse implement first?
option1: Administer the scheduled oral statin for an LDL level of 184 mg/dL
option2: Arrange a dietary consultation for a sodium-restricted meal plan
option3: Collect the scheduled fasting lipid panel before beginning treatment
option4: Begin the prescribed titratable IV antihypertensive with frequent BP reassessment
rationale: Treating the emergency BP and limiting further organ injury take priority over lipid testing, statin administration, and dietary teaching. True hypertensive emergencies generally require monitored IV treatment; the oral-drug example in the course case should not be generalized to all emergencies. (Source: Ch31 slides 121–122; teacher outline: priority sequencing; AHA 2024 clinical clarification.)

question: A client with BP 186/118 mm Hg has glucose 248 mg/dL, LDL 181 mg/dL, BUN 34 mg/dL, creatinine 2.4 mg/dL (baseline 1.0), and new urine protein. Which finding most directly supports acute renal involvement?
option1: The elevated LDL together with the elevated blood glucose
option2: The creatinine increase together with new protein in the urine
option3: The systolic BP together with a family history of hypertension
option4: The elevated glucose together with a history of cigarette smoking
rationale: A rising creatinine and new proteinuria point to impaired kidney function and renal injury. Hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia, smoking, and family history increase vascular risk but do not by themselves demonstrate acute renal dysfunction. (Source: Ch31 slides 27, 118; teacher outline: full data-set interpretation.)

question: During treatment of a hypertensive emergency, BP improves to the prescribed range. The client becomes harder to arouse, and urine output falls from 45 to 12 mL in the last hour. What is the nurse's best response?
option1: Document that the BP goal has been reached and continue routine observations
option2: Encourage sleep because fatigue is expected when the BP begins to decrease
option3: Immediately reassess perfusion and alert the treating team about the deterioration
option4: Offer additional oral fluids and wait for the next scheduled laboratory results
rationale: A better BP number does not establish adequate organ perfusion. Decreasing alertness and oliguria indicate possible worsening cerebral and renal perfusion and need prompt evaluation. Oral fluids or delayed reassessment do not address the acute change. (Source: Ch31 slides 27, 123, 130–131; teacher outline: evaluating response.)

question: A client says, "My BP has been normal for a week, so I will take my medication only when I get a headache." Which response is best?
option1: Checking for a headache is a reasonable way to decide when the next dose is needed
option2: Normal readings may reflect treatment; continue the prescribed schedule and follow the provider's hold instructions
option3: Skip medication on normal-BP days and take an extra dose if the pressure rises
option4: After a week of normal readings, lifestyle measures can replace the prescription
rationale: Hypertension is often asymptomatic, and controlled readings may mean the medication is working. Consistent use, within prescribed parameters, helps prevent organ injury. Symptom-based dosing, doubling doses, or stopping without guidance can disrupt control. (Source: Ch31 slides 25, 29, 125; teacher outline: adherence.)

question: A client started on antihypertensive therapy feels dizzy immediately after standing. The nurse assists the client back to a safe seated position. Which teaching should follow?
option1: Sit at the bedside before standing and rise slowly with assistance if dizzy
option2: Avoid walking during the day so the medication can reach its full effect
option3: Take the next dose early to prevent another episode of dizziness
option4: Restrict all fluids for the rest of the day to stabilize the circulation
rationale: Slow position changes reduce falls associated with orthostatic symptoms. Ongoing symptoms require assessment, but prolonged inactivity, an extra or early dose, and indiscriminate fluid restriction do not correct the problem and may worsen risk. (Source: Ch31 slides 124; teacher outline: orthostatic safety.)

question: A client is prescribed the course's 1,600-mg daily sodium limit. Breakfast contained 350 mg, lunch 480 mg, and a snack 170 mg. Which dinner meets the remaining daily allowance?
option1: A dinner labeled as containing 640 mg of sodium
option2: A dinner labeled as containing 720 mg of sodium
option3: A dinner labeled as containing 810 mg of sodium
option4: A dinner labeled as containing 560 mg of sodium
rationale: The client has consumed 350 + 480 + 170 = 1,000 mg, leaving 600 mg. The 560-mg dinner gives a daily total of 1,560 mg. Each other dinner would exceed the specifically prescribed 1,600-mg limit. (Source: Ch31 slides 28–29; teacher outline: DASH sodium target.)

question: A client asks why years of poorly controlled hypertension can eventually weaken the left ventricle. Which explanation is most accurate?
option1: The ventricle receives less venous blood because hypertension consistently lowers circulating volume
option2: The ventricle pumps against increased resistance, which can cause remodeling and eventual dysfunction
option3: The ventricle stops relaxing because high BP prevents the atrioventricular valves from opening
option4: The ventricle becomes weaker because hypertension initially eliminates its need to contract forcefully
rationale: Chronic elevation of vascular resistance increases afterload and cardiac workload. Over time, ventricular remodeling can progress to impaired pumping. This mechanism is not explained by reliably decreased circulating volume, valve closure, or reduced work. (Source: Ch31 slides 24, 26; teacher outline: hypertension complications.)

question: A 68-year-old client has high LDL, smokes daily, rarely exercises, and has a parent who died of a stroke. Which plan best addresses modifiable atherosclerosis risks?
option1: Focus on the family history because inherited risk makes lifestyle changes ineffective
option2: Delay changes until leg pain or chest pain confirms that plaque is affecting blood flow
option3: Set a smoking-cessation plan, increase appropriate activity, and follow lipid-lowering treatment
option4: Replace the statin with exercise once the client can walk without shortness of breath
rationale: Smoking, activity, and dyslipidemia are modifiable risks. Age and family history cannot be changed, but they do not make prevention futile. Atherosclerosis can be asymptomatic; medication changes should not be made solely because exercise is tolerated. (Source: Ch31 slides 3, 7, 14; teacher outline: risk factors.)

question: Repeated measurements show right-arm BP 166/90 mm Hg and left-arm BP 138/84 mm Hg. The left radial pulse is weaker. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
option1: The difference is an expected age-related finding that does not require documentation
option2: The lower left-arm reading proves that the systemic hypertension has resolved
option3: The pattern most strongly indicates venous valve failure in the left arm
option4: The pattern suggests arterial narrowing affecting the left arm and needs further evaluation
rationale: A persistent systolic difference of 28 mm Hg with a weaker pulse suggests impaired arterial inflow on the lower-pressure side. The slides identify differences greater than 15–20 mm Hg as concerning for subclavian stenosis. This is not diagnostic by itself. (Source: Ch31 slides 12, 45; teacher outline: arterial narrowing.)

question: While assessing a client with vascular disease, a student prepares to palpate both carotid arteries at the same time. What should the supervising nurse do?
option1: Stop the maneuver and assess one carotid artery at a time
option2: Allow the maneuver because equal bilateral pressure improves pulse comparison
option3: Ask the student to press more firmly to distinguish a pulse from a bruit
option4: Replace pulse assessment with a calf circumference measurement
rationale: The slides specifically caution against simultaneous carotid palpation because it can compromise cerebral blood flow. Assess one side at a time and auscultate for bruits; a bruit is a sound, not something identified by firmer palpation. (Source: Ch31 slides 12; teacher outline: vascular assessment.)

question: A client reports calf cramping after walking two blocks. The discomfort resolves within several minutes of stopping and returns at about the same walking distance. The foot is cool with diminished pulses. Which condition best explains the pattern?
option1: Chronic venous insufficiency producing dependent edema
option2: An acute deep vein thrombosis producing venous obstruction
option3: Peripheral arterial disease producing intermittent claudication
option4: A ruptured aortic aneurysm producing sudden blood loss
rationale: Reproducible exertional calf pain relieved by rest is intermittent claudication. Cool skin and diminished pulses further support arterial insufficiency. Venous pain more often accompanies edema and dependency; the described stable pattern does not suggest acute rupture or DVT. (Source: Ch31 slides 34, 45; study guide: PAD versus CVI.)

question: For an ABI assessment, the higher right-ankle systolic pressure is 84 mm Hg. Brachial systolic pressures are 140 mm Hg on the right and 126 mm Hg on the left. Which result should the nurse report?
option1: ABI 0.67, showing normal arterial perfusion
option2: ABI 0.60, supporting peripheral arterial disease
option3: ABI 1.50, supporting normal venous valve function
option4: ABI 1.67, confirming deep vein thrombosis
rationale: Use the higher brachial pressure: 84 / 140 = 0.60. This is below the slide threshold of 0.9 and supports PAD. ABI evaluates arterial perfusion; it does not diagnose DVT or measure venous valve function. (Source: Ch31 slides 35–36, 45; teacher outline: ABI.)

question: A client with PAD says foot pain now wakes them from sleep and occurs even without walking. A toe ulcer has not healed. Which interpretation should the nurse prioritize?
option1: An expected effect of improved collateral circulation requiring reassurance
option2: Uncomplicated intermittent claudication requiring only scheduled rest breaks
option3: Isolated venous insufficiency requiring immediate high-pressure compression
option4: Progression to severe chronic ischemia requiring prompt vascular evaluation
rationale: Rest pain and nonhealing ulceration suggest sustained severe arterial insufficiency, beyond uncomplicated exertional claudication. The slides associate these findings with critical limb ischemia and risk of tissue loss. Compression should not be initiated indiscriminately in severe arterial disease. (Source: Ch31 slides 42, 44; study guide: arterial ulcers.)

question: A client with known arterial insufficiency reports increased foot pain when the nurse places both legs on pillows above heart level. Which action is most appropriate?
option1: Lower the affected leg to a slightly dependent position and reassess pain and perfusion
option2: Add another pillow to increase the pressure gradient for venous drainage
option3: Apply a tight elastic wrap before lowering the foot to mattress level
option4: Keep the legs elevated until the pain resolves because pallor is expected
rationale: A slightly dependent position can support arterial flow in PAD. Elevation above the heart may worsen ischemic pain and pallor. Tight wrapping may further compromise flow; persistent or worsening pain still requires assessment. (Source: Ch31 slides 38, 46; teacher outline: arterial positioning.)

question: One hour after femoral artery angioplasty, a client develops sudden severe foot pain and numbness. The foot is pale and cold, and the previously detectable pedal Doppler signal is absent. What should the nurse do first?
option1: Elevate the limb above heart level and reassess in one hour
option2: Notify the vascular team immediately for suspected acute limb ischemia
option3: Encourage the client to walk to improve collateral circulation
option4: Administer the PRN analgesic and defer reassessment until it takes effect
rationale: New pain, sensory change, pallor, coldness, and loss of a previously present signal indicate an acute perfusion emergency after intervention. Urgent vascular evaluation is needed to protect the limb. Waiting for analgesia, walking, or elevation delays treatment. (Source: Ch31 slides 40–42, 45; teacher outline: postprocedure acute limb ischemia.)

question: A client with PAD has reduced sensation in both feet. Which statement indicates that discharge teaching has been understood?
option1: I will check my feet only when they hurt because pain is the earliest sign of injury
option2: I will cross my legs while seated to keep pressure off the bottoms of my feet
option3: I will wait until my next monthly visit to mention a new sore if it is painless
option4: I will inspect the soles and between my toes every day and report new skin breaks
rationale: Daily inspection includes soles and spaces between toes because reduced sensation can hide injury. New skin breakdown needs timely attention in poorly perfused tissue. Crossing legs can further impair circulation, and absence of pain does not establish safety. (Source: Ch31 slides 47; study guide: PAD nursing care.)

question: A client with PAD asks why both clopidogrel and a statin are prescribed. Which explanation best connects the medications to the disease?
option1: Clopidogrel reduces platelet aggregation, while the statin addresses lipid-related vascular risk
option2: Clopidogrel dissolves established plaque, while the statin immediately opens blocked arteries
option3: Clopidogrel repairs venous valves, while the statin prevents lower-leg fluid pooling
option4: Clopidogrel replaces activity therapy, while the statin eliminates the need to stop smoking
rationale: The drugs address different contributors to atherosclerotic disease: platelet-related clot formation and lipid-related risk. Neither immediately removes an established obstruction, repairs venous valves, or replaces exercise and smoking cessation. (Source: Ch31 slides 39, 46; teacher outline: PAD management.)

question: The nurse must decide which client needs urgent follow-up. Which finding is most concerning?
option1: A client with stable claudication who stops briefly during a prescribed walk
option2: A client with venous insufficiency whose ankle swelling decreases with elevation
option3: A client with PAD whose toe ulcer has enlarged and developed black tissue
option4: A client after PAD teaching who reports inspecting both feet each evening
rationale: An enlarging ulcer with black tissue suggests tissue necrosis from severe ischemia and threatens limb viability. Stable exertional symptoms, reduced venous edema, and daily foot inspection do not indicate the same deterioration. (Source: Ch31 slides 9, 42, 47; study guide: arterial versus venous findings.)

question: A client with carotid stenosis calls the clinic after a 10-minute episode of slurred speech and left-arm weakness that has now resolved. Which instruction is best?
option1: Schedule a routine follow-up because symptom resolution excludes a stroke risk
option2: Take the next statin dose early and call back if symptoms last more than an hour
option3: Rest at home and avoid reporting another episode unless consciousness is lost
option4: Seek emergency evaluation now because transient deficits may be a TIA
rationale: Transient focal deficits may represent a TIA and warn of stroke risk even when they resolve. Prompt emergency evaluation is appropriate. Waiting for prolonged symptoms or loss of consciousness can delay time-sensitive care. (Source: Ch31 slides 53, 59, 66; teacher outline: stroke warning signs.)

question: Two hours after carotid endarterectomy, the nurse notes increasing neck swelling, stridor, and falling oxygen saturation. Which action has priority?
option1: Place the head in a neutral position and recheck the incision at the next observation
option2: Test tongue movement and shoulder strength before contacting the surgical team
option3: Activate emergency assistance and prepare for airway management while notifying the surgeon
option4: Encourage oral fluids to loosen secretions and reassess the breathing sounds
rationale: An expanding neck hematoma can compress the trachea after CEA. Stridor and falling oxygen saturation require immediate airway-focused escalation. Positioning and cranial nerve checks matter, but they must not delay management of threatened ventilation. (Source: Ch31 slides 62; study guide: post-CEA complications.)

question: After carotid endarterectomy, a client has clear breath sounds, stable oxygen saturation, and no neck swelling, but develops new hoarseness and coughs when offered water. Which action is best?
option1: Continue thin liquids in larger sips to determine whether coughing improves
option2: Stop oral intake, assess swallowing and airway safety, and notify the provider
option3: Document the changes as expected and resume the regular diet
option4: Keep the head turned toward the incision during feeding
rationale: New hoarseness and swallowing difficulty may reflect vagus nerve involvement after CEA and create aspiration risk. Stop intake and obtain prompt evaluation. Stable oxygen saturation does not prove swallowing is safe, and larger sips increase risk. (Source: Ch31 slides 62; study guide: cranial nerve X.)

question: The nurse checks cranial nerve function after carotid endarterectomy. Which assessment combination best matches the nerves emphasized in the teacher outline?
option1: Ask the client to smile, assess voice and swallowing, shrug shoulders, and protrude the tongue
option2: Check pupil size, visual acuity, hearing, and the patellar reflex
option3: Check near vision, extraocular movements, ankle strength, and smell
option4: Assess the plantar reflex, grip strength, hearing, and abdominal sensation
rationale: The outline emphasizes VII, X, XI, and XII: facial movement; voice/swallowing; shoulder shrug; and tongue movement. Other neurologic checks can be valuable, but the alternate combinations do not specifically assess this set. (Source: Ch31 slides 62; teacher outline and study guide: post-CEA cranial nerves.)

question: After carotid artery stenting, a client's BP falls to 82/48 mm Hg with new lightheadedness. The airway is patent, SpO2 is 97%, and lungs are clear. Which action is appropriate while the provider is urgently notified?
option1: Raise the head of the bed to 90 degrees and restrict all IV fluids
option2: Administer the scheduled antihypertensive to reduce carotid stimulation
option3: Position the client flat as tolerated and prepare prescribed fluids or vasoactive support
option4: Assist the client to walk and reassess the pressure after activity
rationale: Post-carotid hypotension can compromise cerebral perfusion. With no respiratory contraindication described, the course recommends flat positioning and anticipated fluid or vasoactive support. Antihypertensive medication and upright activity may worsen the hypotension. (Source: Ch31 slides 62, 64; teacher outline: postprocedure BP.)

question: After carotid endarterectomy, BP is 184/102 mm Hg, above the surgeon's ordered range. The client is alert with no new focal deficits. Which plan is most appropriate?
option1: Keep the head neutral with the head of bed at 30 degrees and implement prescribed BP control
option2: Place the client flat and administer a routine fluid bolus to increase cerebral flow
option3: Rotate the head away from the incision and delay treatment until symptoms appear
option4: Allow the pressure to remain elevated because it always improves cerebral perfusion
rationale: Post-carotid BP must stay within ordered parameters to protect the repair and cerebral circulation. The slides recommend 30-degree head elevation for hypertension and a neutral head after CEA. Excess BP is not harmless merely because the examination is currently stable. (Source: Ch31 slides 64–65; teacher outline: postprocedure BP.)

question: A client with chronic kidney disease returns from carotid artery stenting. The client has no fluid restriction or signs of overload. Which addition to routine neurologic and access-site monitoring is most appropriate?
option1: Restrict fluids until the contrast has been completely eliminated
option2: Use normal pedal pulses as evidence that kidney monitoring is unnecessary
option3: Focus only on cranial nerve XII because no contrast is used during stenting
option4: Trend urine output and creatinine and maintain the prescribed hydration plan
rationale: Contrast exposure makes renal monitoring particularly important after CAS, especially with existing kidney disease. Follow the individualized hydration plan and watch urine output and renal trends. Peripheral pulses do not assess kidney function, and fluids should not be arbitrarily restricted. (Source: Ch31 slides 62, 65; teacher outline: CAS renal priorities.)

question: A client with active cancer develops a DVT after abdominal surgery and several days of limited mobility. Which explanation correctly applies Virchow's triad?
option1: Cancer causes stasis, surgery lowers coagulability, and immobility directly tears arterial walls
option2: Cancer increases coagulability, surgery can injure endothelium, and immobility causes stasis
option3: Cancer repairs endothelium, surgery increases venous return, and immobility lowers platelet activity
option4: Cancer and immobility affect only arterial plaque, while surgery causes venous valve repair
rationale: The three contributors are hypercoagulability, endothelial injury, and venous stasis. Active cancer, surgery, and immobility respectively illustrate these mechanisms and explain why combined risks increase the likelihood of DVT. (Source: Ch31 slides 88–89; teacher outline: Virchow's triad.)

question: A postoperative client develops a newly swollen, warm, tender left calf. Which nursing action is most appropriate?
option1: Compare both legs, notify the provider, and prepare for ordered compression ultrasonography
option2: Massage the tender area and reassess after the muscle relaxes
option3: Perform repeated forceful ankle dorsiflexion to confirm a positive Homan sign
option4: Apply an SCD to the symptomatic leg while awaiting the next routine assessment
rationale: New unilateral swelling, warmth, and tenderness raise concern for DVT. Compare findings and obtain prompt evaluation with appropriate imaging. Homan sign is unreliable; massage and mechanical compression of the suspicious limb are not appropriate diagnostic responses. (Source: Ch31 slides 91–92, 99–100; teacher outline: DVT recognition.)

question: Ultrasound confirms an acute DVT in a client's left leg. Which order should the nurse clarify before implementation?
option1: Administer the prescribed anticoagulant after required safety checks
option2: Monitor for hematuria, bloody stool, and falling hemoglobin
option3: Elevate the affected leg when resting as prescribed
option4: Apply sequential compression to the left leg
rationale: The course specifically identifies SCD use on a limb with a confirmed acute DVT as an order requiring clarification. Anticoagulation, bleeding surveillance, and appropriate resting elevation are consistent with the chapter's management plan. (Source: Ch31 slides 99–100; teacher outline: SCD safety.)

question: A client with unilateral calf swelling has an elevated D-dimer after recent surgery. Which interpretation is most accurate?
option1: The result proves the clot is in the symptomatic calf and makes ultrasound unnecessary
option2: The result distinguishes a deep venous clot from an arterial embolus without other testing
option3: The result does not confirm DVT; imaging is needed because other conditions can elevate D-dimer
option4: The result proves a pulmonary embolism is present even without respiratory findings
rationale: D-dimer reflects fibrin breakdown and can be elevated for reasons other than DVT, including recent surgery. It does not locate a clot or independently establish DVT or PE. Compression ultrasound is used to evaluate suspected leg DVT. (Source: Ch31 slides 92, 99; NHLBI: DVT diagnostic clarification.)

question: A hospitalized client with a proximal DVT suddenly develops dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, HR 124/min, and SpO2 86%. Which action should the nurse take first?
option1: Increase leg elevation and reassess the oxygen saturation in 30 minutes
option2: Activate emergency assistance and provide oxygen while urgently assessing for pulmonary embolism
option3: Encourage a hallway walk to reduce venous stasis before calling the provider
option4: Give the next scheduled oral anticoagulant and wait for symptom improvement
rationale: Acute hypoxemia and cardiopulmonary symptoms in a client with DVT suggest PE. Emergency escalation and oxygenation take priority. Leg positioning and scheduled medication do not address the immediate threat to gas exchange and circulation. (Source: Ch31 slides 90, 96, 99; teacher outline: DVT-to-PE connection.)

question: A client receiving IV unfractionated heparin for DVT has aPTT above the protocol range, new gross hematuria, and hemoglobin that falls from 12.1 to 9.2 g/dL. Which response is best?
option1: Continue the infusion because a prolonged aPTT is always the desired treatment response
option2: Increase the infusion because hematuria indicates that the clot is dissolving
option3: Wait for the next scheduled laboratory draw because bruising is the only serious bleeding sign
option4: Stop or hold the infusion per bleeding protocol and notify the provider immediately
rationale: The combination of visible bleeding, falling hemoglobin, and excessive anticoagulation needs immediate intervention under protocol. Some prolongation may be therapeutic, but a value above range with bleeding is not a successful outcome. Hematuria is not evidence of clot dissolution. (Source: Ch31 slides 94, 99, 101; study guide: DVT care.)

question: A stable client with DVT has started therapeutic anticoagulation and is cleared to ambulate. Which statement indicates a need for further teaching?
option1: I will take my anticoagulant as prescribed and keep required follow-up appointments
option2: I should stay in bed until every trace of the clot has disappeared
option3: I will take movement breaks and do leg exercises during long trips
option4: I will report blood in my urine or stool while taking this medication
rationale: The chapter supports appropriate early ambulation rather than routine prolonged bed rest. This client has been treated and cleared for activity. Adherence, movement during travel, and recognition of bleeding are appropriate teaching points. (Source: Ch31 slides 100–102; teacher outline: DVT management.)

question: A client has chronic ankle edema, brown lower-leg pigmentation, and a shallow draining ulcer near the medial ankle. The foot is warm and pedal pulses are present. Which condition best fits?
option1: Chronic venous insufficiency
option2: Acute peripheral arterial occlusion
option3: Rupture of an abdominal aortic aneurysm
option4: Isolated carotid artery stenosis
rationale: Edema, brown pigmentation, a shallow medial-ankle ulcer, warmth, and preserved pulses favor venous insufficiency. Arterial disease more often produces coolness, reduced pulses, and distal ischemic ulcers. The other conditions do not explain this local chronic pattern. (Source: Ch31 slides 103–105, 113; study guide: PAD versus CVI.)

question: A client with chronic venous insufficiency stands at work for long periods. Arterial perfusion has been assessed as adequate, and compression is prescribed. Which plan best addresses the cause of the symptoms?
option1: Keep the legs dependent throughout the evening and avoid compression
option2: Remain completely inactive after work to prevent calf-muscle contraction
option3: Use prescribed compression, take movement breaks, and elevate the legs when resting
option4: Reduce skin care because covering the skin prevents venous drainage
rationale: Venous valve failure promotes pooling. Prescribed compression, calf-muscle activity, avoidance of prolonged standing, and elevation support venous return and reduce edema. Dependency and inactivity worsen pooling; skin care protects vulnerable tissue. (Source: Ch31 slides 104, 107, 114–115; teacher outline: CVI management.)

question: A client labeled as having venous insufficiency is scheduled for a compression wrap. Today the foot is cold and pale, pedal pulses are absent, and pain worsens with elevation. What should the nurse do?
option1: Apply the wrap more tightly because absent pulses indicate excess venous pooling
option2: Withhold the wrap and obtain prompt evaluation of arterial perfusion
option3: Elevate the foot higher and wait until tomorrow to reassess the pulses
